name: Karl Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Karl, I'm 27, and I manage the arable side of the Brandt farm, about 620 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape. There's a small flock of sheep that grazes the cover crops in winter, but grain is the business. I run a team of three, plus two students at harvest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In autumn it's drilling, which means sowing the seed, from first light until the dew comes down. I check every field on foot before I let a machine on it, because the soil tells you more than any screen. In July I'm on the combine and on the phone to the grain merchant at the same time, trying not to sell too early. The part I love is walking a crop in May when it's coming up even. The part that wears me out is the paperwork and the subsidy forms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Lena in a rented cottage on Mill Lane. She teaches at the primary school in town. I don't use AI at all, honestly. Mr Brandt bought a yield-mapping system and I let the younger lad, Tobias, look after it. We've got about four months of money put by, which feels fine until the car needs a clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've been telling Tobias for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. The salesmen at the autumn show promised AI would farm the whole place, and in the end it helps fill in the subsidy forms and that's it. A good grain crop still comes from someone who knows which corner of the field holds water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, and a bit smug. I've never liked being told I'm behind because I won't use a chatbot. If it comes to nothing, the skills I've got are still the skills that count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep the same rotation, keep the team together, and maybe let Tobias use the form-filling tool if it saves me a Sunday. Lena and I would keep saving for a deposit on a house, maybe in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting the last of the wheat in the store the day before the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would notice the difference most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tobias, because he's the one who believes in all of it. He'd be disappointed, and I'd feel a bit bad for him. He's a good lad, he just reads too much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let him use the tool for the forms. So you'd use AI after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd let him use it, I wouldn't touch it myself. If it means I'm out in the field instead of at the kitchen table on a Sunday, I can live with that much.

S0.say: I'd say the salesmen promised AI would farm the whole place and it ended up filling in subsidy forms. A good crop still comes from someone who knows which corner of the field holds water.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved and a bit smug. I've never liked being told I'm behind for not using a chatbot, and this would prove my skills still count.
S0.do: Keeps the same rotation and keeps his team of three together. Lets his colleague Tobias use an AI tool for subsidy forms but won't use it himself, and keeps saving with Lena for a house deposit in about three years.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased, like getting the harvest in before the rain.
S0.quote: A good grain crop still comes from someone who knows which corner of the field holds water.
S0.fieldNote: Karl's whole identity rests on hands-on knowledge of the land, and this scenario confirms it. He admits a small contradiction about letting Tobias use AI, then settles it by keeping his own hands off the tool. His pleasure is partly about being proven right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one sounds more like real life, unfortunately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say the change has to be fair. If machines take the driving and the spraying, the money they save should go into wages and training, not straight to the machinery companies and the big landowners. I'd say that at the farmers' union meeting and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be the one left behind. Tobias would end up running the drones and the self-driving tractor, and I'd be the old-fashioned one at 27. That's a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly, not just pay the fee, and push for a training fund. I'd probably have to do a course on the robot sprayer, even though I'd hate it. I'd also stop thinking about buying a house for a year and keep the four months of savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing the weather turn when you've still got barley standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually have to learn, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting the routes for a self-driving tractor, probably, and reading the maps it makes. Mr Brandt would pay for the course, he's fair like that. I'd sit at the back of the class with my arms folded, but I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machinery firms and the people who own the land. Mr Brandt is decent, but the estate next door already let two men go when they got GPS steering. Nobody asked those men what they thought, and nobody helped them find anything else.

S1.say: I'd say the change has to be fair, and the money saved by machines should go into wages and training. I'd say it at the farmers' union meeting, not just online.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd be the one left behind, with Tobias running the drones while I'm the old-fashioned one at 27. It's a strange thing to admit.
S1.do: Becomes an active member of the farmers' union and pushes for a training fund. Takes a course on the robot sprayer and self-driving tractor, paid by his employer, and pauses house plans for a year to keep his four months of savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy and a little embarrassed, like watching the weather turn with barley still standing.
S1.quote: Tobias would end up running the drones and the self-driving tractor, and I'd be the old-fashioned one at 27. That's a strange thing to admit.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's public line is about fairness for workers, but his private fear is personal: being overtaken by a younger colleague. He would retrain, but reluctantly and with his arms folded. He blames machinery firms and landowners, and has a specific memory of two men let go next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two harvests. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in, and fast. Wages for people whose jobs are gone, and land kept in local hands, not bought up by whoever owns the robots. I'd be the one at the town hall meeting standing up and saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished as a farm manager. If a machine can walk a field and read the soil as well as I can, Mr Brandt doesn't need me, and he'd be stupid to keep paying me. Two years isn't long enough for me to become anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't food and rent, right away. I'd push the union to demand a basic income for farm workers and I'd sign up for every protest. I'd probably also ask Mr Brandt straight out whether I've got a job in 2029, so I'm not the last to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I don't sleep well as it is in harvest. This would be every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I don't know what I'm for anymore. She'd say teaching is safe, and I'd say nothing is safe in that picture. Then we'd sit in the kitchen and not watch the television.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got four months saved. How far does that go in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nowhere, really. It's enough to cover a gap between jobs, not a gap between lives. Lena's pay would carry us for a while, and I'd hate that, but I'd be grateful.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in fast, with wages for people whose jobs are gone and land kept in local hands. I'd stand up at the town hall meeting and say it.
S2.think: Privately I think I'm finished as a farm manager, because a machine that reads the soil as well as me makes me a cost. Two years isn't long enough to become anything else.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food and rent at once. Pushes the farmers' union to demand a basic income for farm workers, joins protests, and asks his employer directly whether he has a job in 2029.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, like the worst nights of harvest every night.
S2.quote: It's enough to cover a gap between jobs, not a gap between lives.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning Karl sees no personal escape route, so his energy goes into collective demands. He's frank that his partner's teaching pay would carry them, and that he'd feel both shame and gratitude. His resistance to new tools leaves him with nothing to pivot to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Five harvests. I'd still be 32 when it hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but louder and earlier. We've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan for rural people. I'd be writing to our local member of parliament every few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes me feel worse in a way. With two years you just get hit. With five, people will say I had time and didn't use it, and they'd be right, because I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year arguing and the second year doing something. Maybe I'd train as a teacher like Lena, because a classroom feels like the last place they'd send a robot. I'd save harder too, and try to get to six months instead of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like knowing the combine is going to break down, just not which week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching? Tell me more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've had students on the farm every summer and I like it, showing them how to judge when barley's ready by biting a grain. Lena says I'm patient with them in a way I'm not with machines. It's a real thought, not just panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those five years look like on the farm itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Brandt would buy the robots in year three or four, when the price drops. I'd probably end up training the robots' supervisor, which is a strange job to do on your way out. I'd do it properly, though, because the land deserves that.

S3.say: I'd say there's no excuse for the government not having a plan for rural people with five years' warning. I'd write to our local member of parliament every few months.
S3.think: Privately, five years feels worse in a way, because people will say I had time and didn't use it. They'd be right, because I'd drag my feet at first.
S3.do: Lobbies his local member of parliament and argues for a rural plan in the first year. Starts looking at retraining as a teacher in the second year and saves harder to reach six months of expenses.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a slow dread like waiting for a machine to break down.
S3.quote: With two years you just get hit. With five, people will say I had time and didn't use it, and they'd be right, because I'd drag my feet.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't comfort Karl; it adds guilt, because he expects to resist for too long. Teaching came up as a genuine idea rooted in his summer students, not just panic. He'd still treat the land with care even while training his replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it to make sure farm workers share in what the machines earn. Co-operatives, worker shares in the robots, that kind of thing. I'd say it at the union and probably at the pub as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I can still have most of my career doing what I love. That's selfish, but it's true. By 37 I'd have time to change, and I think by then I'd even be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd carry on as normal and save. Around year five I'd start a teaching qualification part-time, in the winters when the farm is quieter. Lena and I would still buy a house, just a smaller one, and we'd decide about children with the dates in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Like a long-range forecast that says rain, but in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools yourself in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, by the end. Not because I'd want to, but because the teaching job would need it. I'd learn it the way I learned to reverse a trailer, slowly and with a lot of swearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about it properly. Lena wants two. I'd want to know what kind of world they'd go to school in, but I don't know, and nobody does. I think we'd still go ahead.

S4.say: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's make sure farm workers share in what the machines earn. Co-operatives and worker shares in the robots, at the union and at the pub.
S4.think: Privately, ten years means I get most of my career doing what I love. It's selfish but true, and by 37 I think I'd be ready to change.
S4.do: Carries on as normal and saves for the first few years. Starts a part-time teaching qualification in the winters around year five, buys a smaller house with Lena and plans children with the dates in mind.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, with relief at having time.
S4.quote: I'd learn it the way I learned to reverse a trailer, slowly and with a lot of swearing.
S4.fieldNote: For Karl, ten years turns a crisis into a career plan. He'd still delay, but there's room for his slow pace. He links even family decisions to the timeline, while admitting that nobody can say what the world will look like.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is a guarantee that farm workers get paid while they retrain, and that the land isn't bought up by whoever owns the machines. And somebody to show me the new tools slowly, like Mr Brandt showed me the combine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole question for me. If farmers own them together, it's a different story than if one company does.

headlineQuote: It's enough to cover a gap between jobs, not a gap between lives.
portrait: Karl is a 27-year-old arable manager on a 620-hectare grain and oilseed farm who trusts his boots and his eyes more than any screen. He leans left, believes in unions and blames machinery firms and big landowners when workers lose out. He never uses AI and would resist it until there was no choice, which makes the fast scenarios frightening and the slow one a relief. As the warning time grows from 2 to 10 years, his plans shift from protest and cutting back to a slow move towards teaching, alongside his partner Lena.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years isn't long enough for him to become anything else and four months of savings won't cover a whole change of life.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining for farm workers, land kept out of the hands of whoever owns the machines, and someone patient to teach him the new tools.
